title: Two boons, and no third
hookLine: the question is never answered, but omens frighten the blind king, and Draupadi frees her husbands with two boons
carry: lobha: wanting without end wears dharma away
tomorrow: Why go back for one more game?

cards: Draupadi asks one more time. In the telling, she says she has been dragged here and wronged before everyone, and still no one has spoken. Then, once more: am I a slave, or free?
Say it, and I'll accept it. And this time something does answer, though not from the people in the hall. By the end of this long day, a blind king finally speaks.

teach.b: Bhishma answers once more, and again he can't settle it: Yudhishthira alone, he says, should say whether she was won.
Duryodhana, smiling, sets a trap: let the four younger brothers say Yudhishthira wasn't their master, and she'll be free.
Before they answer, Duryodhana makes an insulting gesture toward Draupadi, and Bhima swears a second vow, against him.

Arjuna answers the trap: he was our master when he staked us, but whose master was he once he'd lost himself? Then the sounds begin. A jackal howls in the chamber where the king's sacred fire is kept.

teach.h: THE BLIND KING OFFERS A BOON.
teach.b: Gandhari and Vidura hear it and tell the blind king. And Dhritarashtra, frightened, finally acts. He rebukes his son and offers Draupadi a boon.
She asks for Yudhishthira's freedom, so her son won't be called a slave's son. Granted. A second: that the other four go free, with their weapons and chariots.
Granted. Then he offers a third, and Draupadi refuses.
Greed, she says, wears away dharma. A woman of a warrior's house may ask two boons; her husbands, now free, can win the rest by their own deeds.

That word is lobha, greed, and Hindu teaching counts it among the six inner enemies, beside desire and anger. Notice: asking wasn't the problem. Draupadi asked, and asked well, for exactly what freed the people she loved.
Lobha is the wanting that never stops.
She knew where enough was, and put the asking down.

how: Draupadi's two boons and her refusal of a third are retold as a picture of dignity and of lobha, greed, refused; in parts of south India Draupadi herself is honored as a goddess.

o: a vow Bhima swears against Duryodhana in the hall
a question unanswered, yet her asking freed five brothers
a bargain Duryodhana offers the four younger brothers

games.q: the end of the day — tap the pairs.
p: whose master, once he lost himself?
greed, one of the six inner enemies

s: Draupadi's first boon was Yudhishthira's freedom
she asked it so her son wouldn't be called a slave's son.
he said Yudhishthira alone should answer.
in Hindu teaching, asking God or anyone for things is itself greed
Draupadi asked, and asked well; lobha is wanting that never stops.

games.q: you're Draupadi. the blind king has granted your two boons, and your husbands are free. now he offers you a third. what do you do?
games.why: she refuses: greed wears away dharma, she says, and her freed husbands can win the rest by their own deeds.

practice: Many Hindus begin their own requests with a prayer for everyone: sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy, may all be free from illness. Say it, or its meaning.
Then ask for one or two things you truly need, and stop there, the way Draupadi did. If you pray, offer the rest to God; if you don't, notice what it feels like to want enough.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi's question. Never answered by the hall, yet by the day's end she asks two boons, frees five brothers, and refuses a third.

orig.note: Sanskrit lobha: greed, the wanting that never stops; one of the six inner enemies.

carryVoice: Your line: lobha: wanting without end wears dharma away. Two boons, and no third. Day seven hundred seventy-five, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Draupadi's last appeal; Bhishma says Yudhishthira alone should answer; Duryodhana's challenge to the brothers; Arjuna's reply; Bhima's vow against Duryodhana; the omens in the homa chamber; Dhritarashtra's boons; Draupadi's refusal of a third)
Hindu teaching of the six inner enemies (shadripu: kama, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, matsarya)
